title: History of Clay.com: From a Spreadsheet to a $7.1B GTM Platform (2017 to 2026)
summary: Clay.com history, 2017 to 2026: how Kareem Amin's spreadsheet became a $7.1B GTM platform with Claygent, waterfall enrichment and the GTM engineer role.
body_markdown:
The oldest tables in the world are made of clay. The most famous is **Plimpton 322** , a Babylonian tablet from about 1800 BCE, small enough to hold in one hand, with four columns and fifteen rows of numbers pressed into it. A scribe built a grid, filled the cells, and let the rows do the work. People have been organizing the world that way ever since.


About 3,800 years later, two founders in Brooklyn took the same grid and asked a new question: what if every cell could go out to the internet and bring back an answer? They called the company **Clay** , because you can shape it into anything. It took them five years to find the customer who cared, and four more to reach a **$7.1 billion valuation** , **$100 million in recurring revenue** , **17,000 customers** , and a job title they say they coined: the **GTM engineer** .


This is the complete history of Clay.com, the go-to-market platform, not the material and not the personal CRM that shared its name. It covers the founders' first startup, the wilderness years, the pivot, every funding round, Claygent, the 2026 pricing split, both Sculpt conferences, and what the story teaches anyone building with AI agents. 🧭


> **TL;DR:** Clay, founded in 2017 by Kareem Amin and Nicolae Rusan, spent five years without product-market fit, then, by its own account, grew from **$1M to $100M ARR in about two years** . It raised a **$115M Series D at $7.1B** in September 2026 and says it coined the GTM engineer role.[Build your own sales agents →](https://www.taskade.com/agents)


## What Is Clay? The GTM Platform Worth $7.1 Billion in 2026


Clay is a New York software company whose product lets go-to-market teams find, enrich, and act on data about companies and people. It combines **150+ data providers** , an AI research agent called **Claygent** , and workflow automation in one spreadsheet-like workspace. Clay was founded in **2017** , is led by CEO **Kareem Amin** , and was valued at **$7.1 billion** in September 2026.


In plain terms: a sales or marketing team describes who it wants to reach and why, and Clay assembles the list, fills in the missing facts from many vendors, researches each account with AI, and sends the result to the tools that do the outreach. Clay calls itself *"GTM infrastructure to grow in ways your competitors can't."*

## 🏺 The Prehistory: From Clay Tablets to "Data Is the Moat" (3000 BCE to 2017)


Every sales-data company before Clay sold the same thing: a list. The business model was to own contact data that competitors did not have, and the industry's history is a series of better lists. Clay's founding insight was that by the late 2010s, the list had become a commodity, and the valuable part was what you did with it.


*Rows, quantities, and a seal of approval: a Mesopotamian clay tablet from about 3100 to 2900 BCE that records barley distribution. Photo: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons.*


The table itself is one of the oldest tools people have. Mesopotamian scribes kept accounts in rows and columns pressed into clay, and the ledger, the Rolodex, and the spreadsheet are its descendants. The modern chapter of that story is in our[history of spreadsheets](https://www.taskade.com/blog/spreadsheet-history) . The sales chapter looks like this.


Year Milestone Why it matters to Clay

c. 1800 BCE Plimpton 322, a clay tablet with a four-column number table Rows and columns as a tool for calculation


1841 The Mercantile Agency, later Dun & Bradstreet, sells credit reports on businesses Company data becomes a product


1950s The Rolodex puts a contact list on every desk A salesperson's value is the names they hold

1999 **Salesforce** launches CRM in the browser The system of record moves online


2000 ZoomInfo's predecessor starts crawling the web for contacts Contact data scales past the phone book


2003 LinkedIn launches People publish their own professional data

2010 Salesforce buys Jigsaw, a crowdsourced contact database Data is treated as a strategic moat


2011 to 2015 SalesLoft, Outreach, Clearbit, and Apollo arrive Sequencers and enrichment APIs for the SDR era


2017 **Clay is founded** in New York A spreadsheet meets the internet's data


By 2017 a typical revenue team paid for a contact database, an enrichment API, a sequencer, a CRM, and a RevOps hire to keep them in sync. Each data vendor claimed the most complete records. Each customer bought two or three of them anyway, because none was complete.


Kareem Amin saw the pattern from outside the sales world, and he described the incumbent logic years later: *"Everybody else in sales and marketing was thinking that the data is the moat."* More users meant more data, which meant a bigger company. Clay, he said, *"flipped it on its head. Data isn't the moat. Data is a commodity. We get data from wherever is needed."*


That flip did not start as a sales idea. It started as a programming idea, and it took the founders years to connect the two.

## 👤 Who Founded Clay? Kareem Amin, Nicolae Rusan, and Varun Anand


Clay was founded in 2017 in Brooklyn, New York, by **Kareem Amin** and **Nicolae Rusan** , two McGill graduates who had already built and sold one startup together. **Varun Anand** joined as an advisor in late 2021, ran operations through the turnaround, and is now recognized as a co-founder. Amin has been CEO since day one. Rusan left in 2022 to start another business, and he was still on Clay's board in 2024.


Several company databases list the wrong founders for Clay, or confuse it with an unrelated personal CRM that used the same name. The record below comes from Clay's own posts, its investors, and interviews with the founders.


Person Role at Clay Before Clay


**Kareem Amin** Co-founder and CEO, 2017 to today McGill, Microsoft, co-founder of Frame, Sailthru, VP of Product at The Wall Street Journal


**Nicolae Rusan** Co-founder, 2017 to 2022, then a board member McGill, Microsoft, co-founder of Frame, Sailthru, VP of Product at Dow Jones


**Varun Anand** Advisor from late 2021, then head of operations, now co-founder Political communications, Google's Jigsaw, insurance startup Newfront


### Kareem Amin: from Dhahran to McGill to Microsoft


Kareem Amin was born in Egypt and grew up in Dhahran, Saudi Arabia, where his father was a hospital doctor. As a teenager he fixed computers for cash. *"It was mostly reinstalling Windows,"* he told Forbes. He studied electrical engineering at McGill University in Montreal, with a serious side interest in physics, and joined Microsoft as a program manager.


The physics never left. He still describes go-to-market as a system with laws, and he quotes Hegel and Feuerbach to explain product strategy. Later in life he added a meditation practice, including ten-day silent retreats, and one of them marks the turning point of this story.


### The first company: The Shared Web, Frame, and a sale he regrets


Amin and Rusan both studied at McGill and both worked at Microsoft. In 2010 they left to start **The Shared Web** , a social news reader, and went through the Techstars Seattle program. The reader did not take off. In 2011 they pivoted to **Frame** , a Shopify app that turned an online store into a tablet storefront.


Email marketing company **Sailthru acquired Frame in May 2012** . The founders spent a year there, then moved to Dow Jones, where Amin became VP of Product at The Wall Street Journal and Rusan held the same title at the parent company. Both left by the end of 2015.


Amin does not count the exit as a win. Asked in 2026 why he kept going through Clay's lean years when he had sold a company before, he said: *"That was just my first attempt, and I think I learned that was a mistake. I wouldn't want to do that."* Clay was built by someone who had already taken the early exit and decided not to take it twice.


### Nicolae Rusan: the co-founder who found the use case


Nicolae Rusan is Canadian, studied computer science, political science, and economics at McGill, and was Clay's product lead in the early years. He wrote the earliest public description of Clay we could find, in January 2017. He also made the call that saved the company. Amin has said so more than once: *"It was actually my co-founder Nicolae who identified this segment and use case."* Amin himself resisted: *"We didn't know much about outbound outreach, but Nicolae decided to try it out."*


Rusan left in 2022 to start another business, and he was still on Clay's board in 2024. Amin gave that account to BetaKit in July 2024. By June 2023 he was posting about a new AI coding project. Clay's current press materials name Amin and Anand, which is why Rusan is missing from many summaries. He belongs in any honest one.


### Varun Anand: the operator who found the customers


Varun Anand came from outside tech's usual pipeline: a political science degree, a stint as a press aide on a presidential campaign, communications at Google's Jigsaw unit, then operations at the insurance startup Newfront. He found Clay as a customer. By one account he joined a Clay webinar and was the only attendee.


He started advising the company in late 2021 and moved into operations in 2022. What he did next is the subject of the "unscalable" chapter below: he joined WhatsApp groups and Slack communities where cold-email agency owners traded tactics, ran about eight calls a day, and sent invoices by hand because, as he later admitted, *"as recently as January 2023, we didn't have billing in the product."*

## 🏜️ The Wilderness Years: Five Products in Search of a User (2017 to 2021)


Clay did not begin as a sales tool. It began in January 2017 as a developer tool for cloud functions, guided by a mission to *"give the power of programming to an order of magnitude more people."* For roughly five years it had funding, smart founders, and no committed customer. Kareem Amin's own accounting of that stretch is two years of building, two years of confusion, and then a decision.


The earliest public description of Clay we could find comes from co-founder Nicolae Rusan, in a post dated January 23, 2017: *"Clay is a layer on top of AWS Lambda"* that makes it easier to get APIs and functions running. A month later Amin published a tutorial that piped those functions into Google Sheets, so live data from an API appeared in a cell. The whole future product is visible in that one demo. It took five years to find out who wanted it.


### What Clay called itself, year by year


Period How Clay described itself Who it was for


2017 "Create cloud hosted microservices" Developers


2018 "The GitHub/Heroku for serverless development" Developers


2019 to 2020 "Workflows, simple DB, and serverless code" for team tools Technical teams


2020 **"The spreadsheet that fills itself"** Anyone with a list


2021 "Automate your prospecting, enrich your customers" Sales and growth teams


2022 "Create spreadsheets that fill themselves, without code" Growth and outbound teams


The team also built and dropped two other ideas along the way: a rebuilt terminal for piping data between tools, and a front-end builder.


### Why a spreadsheet


The founders started with a question about who should get the power. They could make engineers faster, or they could give programming to people who were not engineers. They chose the second. A Clay hiring post from January 2020 states the math: *"about 20 million developers in the world, but over 1 billion spreadsheet users."*


Amin calls the spreadsheet *"the world's most popular programming environment."* One Excel feature fascinated him: **programming by example** . Fix one badly formatted phone number, and the spreadsheet fixes the rest. Correct its one mistake, and it learns the exception. The machine infers the program from what you show it.


From there the idea came as a sequence, each step adding one property to the grid.


Step Product What it added to the spreadsheet


1 VisiCalc and Excel Calculation without code


2 Google Sheets Many people in one grid at once


3 **Clay** Cells connected to all of the internet's data


*"Google made it collaborative,"* Amin told journalist Eric Newcomer, *"but the next step was to make it connected to all of the internet's data."* He remembers the first version as a feeling: *"It's a spreadsheet where, suddenly, data pops up in a cell from somewhere else on the internet."*


Bill Atkinson chased the same goal thirty years earlier with[HyperCard](https://www.taskade.com/blog/hypercard-history) , software built to put the power of the personal computer in the hands of people who do not program. The spreadsheet, the stack of cards, and the connected table are one family of tools: software that non-programmers can still shape.


### Two years building, two years confused


A general tool invites every use case. Recruiters used early Clay. So did salespeople, front-end engineers who wanted a low-code backend, and one customer who used it to transform accounting data. By 2021 about 20 customers paid between $30 and $200 a month. Amin's verdict: *"We had a customer, but it was the wrong customer."*


Investors kept faith. **First Round Capital** led a **$2.5 million seed** in 2017, with boldstart and BoxGroup. **Sequoia** led a **$13.5 million Series A** in 2019. Clay announced neither round at the time. An investor at boldstart recalled the questions he got from colleagues: *"Who are those guys you keep visiting out in Brooklyn? What are they doing?"*


The trap, as Amin describes it, was ambition itself. With venture funding and a big mission, the founders kept asking what the largest possible outcome was, and the answer kept moving as the technology moved. *"We would switch from one manifestation of the idea to another,"* he told Forbes. And to Halligan: *"We would keep changing it to be like, well, if we pointed here, it would be even bigger."*


Brian Halligan, who took HubSpot from zero to a public company, noted that people call Clay *"a seven-year overnight success"* and asked the obvious question: why not quit? Amin's answer was about telling a dip from a dead end. The moment you feel bored, or sure you belong somewhere else, is often *"the cusp of actually getting to the point where it gets interesting."* The voice that says otherwise he called a shape-shifter: it always sounds reasonable, and it is usually avoidance.

## 🔁 The Commitment: Five Decisions That Never Changed


Clay found product-market fit when its founders stopped optimizing for the biggest possible idea and committed to one use case: building lists and researching accounts for go-to-market teams. The decision came between September 2021 and January 2022, and the relaunch on February 8, 2022 hit number one on Product Hunt. Kareem Amin says that once they committed, *"it almost worked instantaneously. It just took some time for everybody else to hear about it."*


The turn has a date. In September 2021, by Forbes's account, Amin went on a ten-day silent meditation retreat with the company at a crossroads. He came back and cut. The code tool went. The workflow product went. Nearly all of the 20 paying customers churned, and some early employees left. Amin describes the feeling precisely: *"When you narrow the scope, it feels claustrophobic."*


The hard part, in Amin's telling, was not technical. Friends considered the two founders among the smartest people they knew. Investors had funded them. Customers were impressed in meetings. Nothing worked, and every month a new technology made a bigger vision possible, so they kept re-aiming. What finally changed was courage: *"We're just going to pick this thing. I don't care how silly it sounds. I don't care about the shame if it fails publicly."* He stopped taking advice, including from customers, because *"if you listen to the wrong people at the time when it's a small idea, you kill it."*


"Instantaneously" needs a footnote. In spring 2022, months after the relaunch, revenue was still close to zero. In May 2022 Clay put its waitlist back up and kept it for 15 months, onboarding users by hand. Revenue then grew about tenfold in 2022 and tenfold again in 2023.


With the use case chosen, Clay locked in five decisions. Amin says they have not changed since, and that almost every later product choice follows from them.


Decision The market norm in sales software What Clay chose


**User** Sell to the frontline rep Build for a technical user


**Name** Call that user an admin or an ops person Call that user a go-to-market engineer


**Product** One button, as simple as possible The most powerful and most flexible tool


**Data** Own a proprietary database Own no data. Be a marketplace for everyone's.


**Pricing** Per seat Per usage


A sixth choice mattered as much to Amin: the product had to be product-led, so a person could sign up and use it without a demo.


Amin credits the method to philosophy class. Hegel described history as thesis, antithesis, and synthesis. Feuerbach took Hegel's system and turned it upside down. The technique, Amin says, is to take what everybody believes, flip it, and follow the flipped version to its natural conclusion: *"Flip everything around, you have a new product."*


### Power over simplicity


The decision that drew the most resistance was the second one. Clay's internal rule is **power and flexibility over simplicity** . Amin is careful about the wording: the team wants simplicity, but *"when they conflict, we give you power, because it's a technical user."*


He explains it with two objects. A microwave should work for anyone: press one minute, press start. A guitar is a tool you learn for life, and someone who has played jazz for ten years still cannot play flamenco. *"If you said, let's build a guitar with three strings because it's easier to use, it seems obviously bad to everyone."* Every "easier Clay" that has launched since is, in his framing, a three-string guitar.


The product-led requirement made everything slower. A powerful tool and a self-serve signup rarely fit together, and Amin says insisting on both is one reason the search took so long. It also explains the customer Clay went looking for first: someone technical enough to *"pick it up and hack around with it."*

## 🧱 How Does Clay Actually Work? Tables, Waterfalls, and Claygent


Clay works like a spreadsheet where every column can run a job. A row is a company or a person. A column fetches data from a provider, runs an AI model, calls an API, or pushes the row to another tool. You build a workflow by adding columns from left to right, then you run it on ten rows, check the output, and run it on ten thousand.


Agency operators who teach the product describe it the same way. One calls Clay *"a canvas where I can interact with all the different tools in my go-to-market tech stack"* in one place. The value is not any single data source. The value is that more than 150 data providers and tools sit one click away from the same row.


### The canonical Clay workflow


Step What the column does Why it exists


**1. Find** Pull a list of companies or people from Clay's search, a CRM, a CSV, or Google Maps Start with a narrow, specific audience


**2. Enrich** Run a **waterfall** across email or phone providers No single vendor covers everyone


**3. Validate** Check each email before it is used Bad addresses wreck sender reputation


**4. Qualify** An AI agent reads the company website and answers a yes or no question Vendor categories are too coarse


**5. Act** Push qualified rows to a sequencer, a CRM, or Slack The table is a means, not the end


```text
A CLAY TABLE, READ LEFT TO RIGHT


+---------+-----------+--------------+-----------+-------------+-------------+
| Company | Contact   | Work email   | Valid?    | B2B?        | Push to     |
| (input) | (input)   | (waterfall)  | (checker) | (AI agent)  | sequencer   |
+---------+-----------+--------------+-----------+-------------+-------------+
| Acme    | J. Rivera | found, #2    | valid     | true        | sent        |
| Bolt Co | S. Chen   | found, #1    | catch-all | false       | skipped     |
| Cedar   | M. Okafor | not found    | skipped   | skipped     | skipped     |
+---------+-----------+--------------+-----------+-------------+-------------+
data in        each column runs only if its condition is true      action out


```


### What is waterfall enrichment?


Waterfall enrichment is Clay's signature mechanic: it asks several data providers the same question in sequence and stops at the first good answer. If provider one has no email for a contact, Clay tries provider two, then three, and validates between steps. You pay for the hit, not for every vendor contract.


The idea sounds obvious now, and every competitor has copied it. It was not what buyers asked for. Kareem Amin recalls customers telling him: *"I just want the number of people that work at a company. I don't care where you're getting it from."* His answer was a travel analogy: you can ask to fly from New York to London in one hour, *"but I can't do that for you. So what's the next best thing?"* The next best thing was every vendor in one place, full transparency, and speed.


### The tricks power users learn first


Three habits separate a Clay beginner from an operator, and all three are about spending less.


- **Run conditions.** Every column can carry a rule such as "only run if the email is valid." A wasted lookup is a wasted credit.
- **Cheap model reads, strong model judges.** Operators scrape a website with an inexpensive model, save the summary, and send only the summary to a stronger model for the decision.
- **Bring your own keys.** Clay lets a customer plug in an existing vendor contract or model key. As Amin told journalist Eric Newcomer, once a customer grows big enough, *"we prefer that they actually have a direct contract"* with the data provider.


That last habit says more about the company than any feature. Most data vendors lock customers in. Clay built an exit ramp into the product on purpose, because its bet was never the data.

## 🤝 Doing Things That Don't Scale: WhatsApp Groups, Reverse Demos, and the First Clay Agencies


Clay's first real market was not software companies. It was the small lead-generation agencies that run outbound campaigns for other businesses. They had the hardest version of the problem, because they solved it for dozens of clients at once, and when Clay worked for them they told everyone. Clay reached them one WhatsApp thread at a time.


Varun Anand did most of the reaching. He joined WhatsApp groups with names like SaaS Yacht Club and Sales Technicians, plus a dozen Slack communities, and answered questions. He ran about eight calls a day. By his count it took roughly seven demos to win one customer paying $200 to $300 a month. Clay removed chat support from the product so that every user had to join one shared Slack, and the support queue became a community.


Amin describes the logic as concentric circles. Agencies sat at the frontier with *"the most complicated set of problems,"* and the same product, with the same features, could then be sold directly to companies. The use case did not change between circles, so each success sold the next one.


### The reverse demo


Clay's early sales call inverted the usual demo. The prospect shared their screen and tried to build something. The Clay team watched, guided when the person got lost, and fixed bugs live. Amin's summary: *"If something broke, we were fixing it in real time while you were on the call."* One call did three jobs: user research, onboarding, and proof that the team cared.


The care was not staged. Co-founder Varun Anand was once helping an agency owner over WhatsApp, and the fix was not landing. Anand said he was coming over to the man's house. The man said not to. Anand went anyway. Amin's telling: *"They became really good friends."* He also explains why it worked: the team was not selling Clay. The pitch was that Clay would help the agency grow, by any means, and *"people are very good people readers."*


### Employee number 11 and the first Clay agency


The clearest picture of this era comes from Eric Nowoslawski, who found Clay early, saw what it could do, and pushed it past its pricing model. As Nowoslawski remembers it, plans were limited by rows before credits existed, so he ran 2,000 rows, exported them, deleted them, and ran 2,000 more. Clay's own pricing history says its first plans were already credit-based, so treat the detail as one user's memory. Anand noticed. His message, as Nowoslawski recalls it: *"The way you're using the product is the way we want everyone to be using the product,"* minus the row-limit trick. He was asked to teach others, then hired. Clay's social lead introduces him as **employee number 11** . First Round's history of the company calls him its third business hire and one of its first ten employees.


Nowoslawski also ran what is described as the first Clay agency, Growth Engine X, and left Clay to scale it. Clay calls him its first agency owner to reach $1 million in annual revenue. By June 2024 Amin counted *"dozens of Claygencies,"* and by January 2026 Clay counted about 150 agencies in its ecosystem. The numbers he shared in 2026 show why an ecosystem formed around the product.

Those are one operator's self-reported figures, not audited results. They still explain the flywheel. A tool that lets one technical person turn seven dollars of data and compute into a three-hundred-dollar outcome will produce agencies, and agencies produce tutorials, templates, case studies, and referrals. Amin compares the pattern to HubSpot, where by his account about half of revenue is touched by a partner.


The oddest customer story Amin tells has nothing to do with sales. A user going through a divorce filmed every item in his house, then used Clay to price each one and estimate its depreciation. It reportedly became a top post on a divorce forum. A general-purpose tool finds uses its makers never planned, which is the point of building one.

## 🤖 What Is Claygent? When LLMs Met the Spreadsheet (2023)


Claygent is Clay's AI research agent. It visits websites, reads them, and returns an answer into a cell, so a team can ask any question about any company and get a structured column back. Clay launched Claygent in **September 2023** on OpenAI's GPT-4, and it passed **one billion runs in June 2025** .


Clay could move that fast because of a choice it made years earlier. Its very first product, in 2017, was a layer on top of **AWS Lambda** , and the habit stuck: every integration in Clay ran as its own function, spun up on demand. Amin's reason was mundane. Junior engineers could write integrations, and *"if they made mistakes, whatever, it won't take the whole product down."* When large language models arrived, a model was one more integration. The developer tool nobody wanted in 2017 became the reason Clay could ship AI research within months of the first capable models.


The product reason mattered more. Data vendors sell a fixed menu, *"here's 50 properties about a company,"* in Amin's words. An agent that researches on demand has no menu. Does this company mention AI in its support docs? Does its site show the logos of our customers? Does it have a remote office in South America? Each answer is a data point no competitor can buy, which is the definition of an edge.


Fixed data vendor Research agent in a cell


A set list of fields Any question you can phrase


The same data sold to every buyer A signal only you thought to ask for


Updated on the vendor's schedule Checked at the moment you run it


Wrong data is the vendor's fault Wrong data is expected, shown, and reviewed


### "The data is going to be wrong"


Clay's most counterintuitive principle is that its data will be wrong, and the product should be designed around that from the first day. Competitors claimed complete, accurate data. Amin's view: *"Everybody knows that's a lie."* Clay promised tools to get data and tools to check it fast.


That one assumption explains a string of product decisions.


- **Session replay was a P0.** Users can watch how Claygent reached an answer, because trust that cannot be assumed has to be earned by showing the work. Collecting feedback on a bad run came with it. Acting on that feedback well was the next priority.
- **A playground and prompt versions.** Users test which prompts work and see which ones stopped working.
- **A second agent can check the first.** One agent collects, another verifies or flags the rows most likely to be wrong.
- **A narrow job.** Claygent researches companies and people, not everything. Amin calls the use case a *"fat long tail,"* narrow enough to write evaluations for.


Amin compared the stance to design software: *"Here's a design tool. You know how to use the line, circle, and a square and you can draw anything."* He also made a philosophical claim that still frames the company. There is no complete, canonical data set of companies and people, *"because they're living entities"* seen from different perspectives. A firm can be B2B, B2C, or both, depending on who is asking.


### What breaks at a billion runs


The failures at scale were not the ones outsiders expect. Amin listed them at a LangChain event in October 2025.

## 🏷️ Naming the Wave: How Clay Created the GTM Engineer


A GTM engineer is a technical operator who treats go-to-market as a system to build, test, and improve, instead of a list of tasks to perform. Clay says it coined the title for its own customer-facing team, and it taught agencies to use it, and stayed quiet while it spread. By 2026 companies including OpenAI, Cursor, Notion, and Lovable employed people with GTM engineering titles.


The title began as an internal naming problem. Clay had people who helped customers design their workflows, and called them customer engineers. Kareem Amin and Varun Anand wanted a name that belonged to Clay. Mike Vernal, the Sequoia partner who led Clay's Series A, had been telling Amin for a while that the company should *own a title* . Amin's answer in the room: *"Let's just call them go-to-market engineers."*


His theory of category creation is short, and it contradicts most advice on the subject.


- **You cannot create a category. You can name one.** *"You can take something that is happening and name it."* The team noticed that the most forward-looking buyers already said "GTM" instead of "sales."
- **Two words stuck together.** The best new terms join two familiar words. Amin's example: try naming a Roomba before the phrase "robot vacuum" exists.
- **Title first, category later.** Clay wanted people to call *themselves* GTM engineers. A person will put a title on a LinkedIn profile long before a market agrees a category exists.
- **Give it fuzzy boundaries.** Clay never published a strict definition. Amin says the meaning is broadening as it should: use a coding agent for go-to-market work and you are doing GTM engineering.
- **Earn the right to claim it.** *"If you go too early and start telling the story, people push back against you."* Clay waited until agencies and operators had made real money under the title.


Brian Halligan, who built the "inbound marketing" category at HubSpot, compared notes with Amin in 2026. HubSpot wrote the book, ran the conference, and attacked an enemy called outbound. Clay did the opposite and stayed in the background. Both companies armed agencies first, for the same reason: an agency needs clients, so it will teach the method in public. ## 🧭 GTM 1.0 to 4.0: The Theory Behind Clay's Bet


The clearest map of Clay's bet is a four-era model of go-to-market that Peter Kang, Clay's social lead, laid out on his own channel in 2026. In each era a new technology makes one resource cheap, and whatever is still scarce becomes the edge. Clay was built for the third era, where data is cheap and judgment is scarce, and it is now building for the fourth. The numbering is Kang's framing, not an official Clay taxonomy.

The first shift is the one Hollywood recorded. In *Glengarry Glen Ross* , the salesmen fight over a stack of index cards because the leads are the business. After the internet, every vendor sold the same contacts to everyone, and the fight moved to plumbing: SDRs, AEs, a CRM, and a dozen tools that RevOps had to keep in sync.


The claim that matters is about where ideas come from. In the 2.0 model, a rep with a good idea files a request with RevOps, RevOps negotiates with engineering, and a quarter later the idea ships or dies. Kang describes what that does to people: it *"trains everyone in the GTM org to not bother."* In the 3.0 model the rep builds a rough version over a weekend, proves it on live deals, and a GTM engineer rebuilds it for scale. ## 🔭 Nine Lessons From the History of Clay


The Clay story compresses into nine lessons for anyone building a product, a category, or a go-to-market team in the age of AI. The common thread is that Clay won by inverting what its market believed, then holding the inversion long enough for the market to catch up.


1. **Commitment beats the biggest idea.** Clay wandered for years chasing the largest possible vision. It worked once the founders picked the opportunity in front of them and stopped re-aiming.
2. **Flip the assumptions and follow them through.** Sell to operators instead of reps, power instead of simplicity, usage instead of seats, a marketplace instead of owned data.
3. **Design for wrong answers.** A product that assumes its data is wrong ships review tools, replays, and transparency. A product that claims perfection ships none of them.
4. **Architecture is strategy in slow motion.** Isolated integrations were built for safety in the 2010s and let Clay ship AI research within months of GPT-4.
5. **Name the wave, do not invent it.** "GTM engineer" described work people were already doing. Clay gave it a title, then earned the right to call it a category.
6. **Serve the hardest users first.** Agencies had the most complex problems and the loudest megaphones.
7. **Match the channel to the product.** A configurable product needs education and community. A creative product needs a creative brand.
8. **Transparency is a pricing strategy.** Clay published its internal reasoning when it changed prices, and treated customers as people who would read it.
9. **A playbook that can be written down is already expiring.** The durable asset is a system that produces the next play.

## 🔮 What's Next for Clay? The $100 Billion Question


Clay enters 2027 as the category leader in go-to-market tooling, with fresh capital, a new agent-first product, and a public debate about whether it can grow fifteenfold again. The open questions are whether agents expand the market the way bulls expect, whether Clay stays the tool those agents choose, and whether a company this flexible can stay simple enough to buy.


**The bull case.** In September 2026, SaaStr founder Jason Lemkin said on the 20VC podcast that he had been *"a Clay skeptic for two years"* and had changed his mind, because *"our agents will only use Clay."* Host Harry Stebbings framed the episode as the bull case for Clay as a $100 billion company. The argument is about the size of the market, not the product. If agents run go-to-market work around the clock, the budget they draw on is not the software budget. It is the payroll budget.


**Clay's own odds.** Peter Kang responded on his channel with a list of what has to be true. Agentic go-to-market has to expand the market by ten to a hundred times, and Clay has to keep winning it, which means agents have to keep preferring Clay on cost, security, reliability, and ease of use. He put the chance, jokingly, at one in fourteen million, and added that nobody inside the company talks about the number. The culture, in his words, is *"let's see how far we can take this."*


**The risks.** Four are visible from outside.


1. **Commoditization.** Every data vendor now offers a waterfall, and a coding agent can rebuild table logic in an afternoon.
2. **Complexity.** Power over simplicity wins operators and loses everyone else. Sculptor and the agent-first builder are Clay's attempt to have both.
3. **Trust with small builders.** The pricing split favored enterprises. The indie operators who made Clay famous noticed.
4. **The Red Queen.** If every team runs the same plays with the same agents, the plays stop working. Clay's own second law says so.


**The model question.** Amin has said that many AI predictions assume models that are one or two orders of magnitude better, and that he has no strong intuition about how close that is. His operating rule is 90% execution and 10% reflection: *"Regardless of what the options are, we will be in a better place the more successful we are right now."*


**The founder's answer.** Asked what he will do when he is old, Amin did not say run a public company. He said he wants to make generative ambient music, sound you cannot quite predict that is still good. It is a fitting ambition for someone who spent five years on a product nobody could predict either. 🔮

What is Clay.com?


Clay is a New York software company that makes a go-to-market platform.
